Write cosx + sinx as √2 sin(x + π/4)

insider_note: This question's sub-integral ∫dx/(sinx+cosx) is the exact building block the very next question (∫ x/(sinx+cosx) dx) also needs — solve this one carefully and the next becomes half the work.

steps.label: Apply the property with a = π/2
steps.margin_note: First two marks. sinx and cosx swap places under x → π/2 − x, so the denominator does not change.
steps.memory_tip: sin(π/2 − x) = cosx and cos(π/2 − x) = sinx — the two swap, so sinx + cosx stays sinx + cosx.
steps.why: Under x → π/2 − x, sinx and cosx exchange roles, so sin²x turns into cos²x while the denominator sinx + cosx is unchanged (it is symmetric in the two).
common_mistakes: Writing sin(π/2 − x) as sinx instead of cosx.
Changing the denominator when it in fact stays the same.

steps.label: Add to reach an x-free integral
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. sin²x + cos²x = 1 is what makes the numerator collapse.
steps.memory_tip: sin²x + cos²x = 1 always — the moment you see both squares added, replace them with 1.
steps.why: Adding the two forms turns the numerator into sin²x + cos²x, which is identically 1, leaving a single integral with no x in the numerator at all.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to replace sin²x + cos²x by 1 and leaving the integral unsimplified.
Dropping the factor of 1/2 when isolating I.

steps.label: Write cosx + sinx as √2 sin(x + π/4)
steps.margin_note: Two marks for the R sin(x+α) rewrite and the cosecant integral.
steps.memory_tip: sinx + cosx = √2 sin(x + π/4) — a standard rewrite, worth memorising outright.
steps.why: Combining sinx and cosx into a single sine wave R sin(x+α) reduces the integral to a standard cosecant form, whose antiderivative is a known log tan formula.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the 1/√2 factors, giving sinx + cosx = sin(x + π/4) with no √2.
Using the wrong standard antiderivative for cosecθ.

steps.label: Evaluate the log limits
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Rationalising the fraction inside the log turns it into a perfect square, which is what makes the final simplification clean.
steps.memory_tip: tan(3π/8) = √2 + 1 and tan(π/8) = √2 − 1 — a pair worth memorising for this whole chapter.
steps.why: Rationalising (√2+1)/(√2−1) by multiplying by (√2+1)/(√2+1) turns the denominator into 1, leaving a perfect square inside the log; log(a²) = 2 log(a) turns that square into a factor of 2, which cancels the outer 1/2 exactly.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as log[(√2+1)/(√2−1)] without rationalising.
Forgetting that log(a²) = 2 log(a), which is what removes the /2 from the coefficient.
